meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'Let It Be Me'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the Everly Brothers. Gilbert Bécaud cut it first as the French "Je t'appartiens," issued December 1955 on La Voix de son Maître.

answer.label: Not an Everly Brothers original — a 1955 Gilbert Bécaud single called “Je t’appartiens”
answer.sourceLine: The Everly Brothers’ 1960 Cadence single is the version almost everyone means by “Let It Be Me,” and it is often assumed to be where the song began. It is not. The song was written and first recorded in French as “Je t’appartiens” by Gilbert Bécaud, who composed the music, with lyrics by Pierre Delanoë; Bécaud’s recording was issued in December 1955 on the French EP 5 – Je t’appartiens (La Voix de son Maître 7 EGF 171) ↗. Manny Curtis wrote the English lyric, and the English version was on American television and on a Columbia single by Jill Corey in 1957, before the Everlys ever cut it.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: His Master's Voice
original.released: Issued in France in December 1955 as the lead track of a 7-inch, 45 rpm EP titled “5 – Je t’appartiens” on La Voix de son Maître (Pathé-Marconi), catalogue 7 EGF 171 — not a two-sided single. The other three tracks were “Ça ! (C’est formidable),” “Pauvre pêcheur” and “Marianne de ma jeunesse,” with orchestra directed by Wal-Berg.
original.charted: No chart placing is documented for Bécaud’s 1955 release; the first chart entry the song is recorded as making anywhere is Jill Corey’s English-language Columbia single, number 57 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1957.
original.writer: Gilbert Bécaud (music) and Pierre Delanoë (French lyrics); Manny Curtis (English lyrics)
original.cover: The Everly Brothers recorded it in New York in December 1959 with producer Archie Bleyer, who had recommended the song to them. Cadence Records released it as a single in 1960, backed with “Since You Broke My Heart.” It reached number 7 on the Billboard Hot 100, number 8 in Canada and number 13 in the UK.

trail: MusicBrainz holds the December 1955 French EP as 5 – Je t’appartiens, La Voix de son Maître 7 EGF 171 ↗, and dates Bécaud’s recording of the song to that release.

The French singles database Encyclopédisque lists the same disc — Je t’appartiens – N°5, December 1955 ↗ — printing the A1 title on the sleeve as “Je t’appartiens ‘Let it be me’” with orchestration by Wal-Berg.

The English Wikipedia article on the song ↗ traces the line from Bécaud and Delanoë through Manny Curtis’s English lyric and Jill Corey’s 1957 Columbia single to the Everly Brothers’ December 1959 New York session and 1960 Cadence release.

authors.name: Gilbert Bécaud
authors.heading: Gilbert Bécaud
authors.bio: Born François Gilbert Léopold Silly in Toulon in 1927, Bécaud was the most physically explosive performer in post-war French popular song — nicknamed “Monsieur 100,000 Volts” for what he did to a stage and to an audience. The Paris Olympia was his home room; he first appeared there in 1954 and returned to it for the rest of his life. He wrote the music for “Je t’appartiens” and recorded it himself, issued in December 1955 on La Voix de son Maître. He also wrote “Et maintenant,” which travelled abroad as “What Now My Love.” He died in Paris in 2001.

authors.name: The Everly Brothers
authors.heading: The Everly Brothers
authors.metaLine: Don Everly 1937–2021 · Phil Everly 1939–2014 · American close-harmony duo
authors.bio: Don and Phil Everly built the close-harmony vocabulary that the Beatles, the Beach Boys and Simon & Garfunkel all borrowed from; Rolling Stone put them at number one on its 2015 list of the greatest duos, and they entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1986. Their “Let It Be Me” was cut in New York in December 1959 with a full studio band and released by Cadence Records in 1960, reaching number 7 on the Billboard Hot 100. Producer Archie Bleyer was the one who put the song in front of them. Nothing about the record is diminished by the fact that it is a cover — the only error is the calendar.

authors.name: Pierre Delanoë
authors.heading: Pierre Delanoë
authors.metaLine: 1918–2006 · French lyricist · French lyrics (English lyrics by Manny Curtis)
authors.bio: Born Pierre Leroyer in Paris in 1918, Delanoë was a tax inspector before he became one of the most prolific lyricists in the French language, credited with several thousand songs for Bécaud, Dalida, Aznavour, Joe Dassin and Michel Sardou, and later a president of SACEM. By the account carried in the song’s Wikipedia entry ↗, he wrote the words as an apology to Bécaud for missing one of his Olympia performances. The English lyric that the Everly Brothers sang is a separate piece of writing, by Manny Curtis.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The Everly Brothers’ 1960 Cadence single is so completely the definitive “Let It Be Me” that the song’s French first life has been almost entirely erased from the popular account. Here is the record.

items.why: Their version, recorded in New York in December 1959 and released by Cadence Records in 1960, reached number 7 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became the reference recording. It is a cover of a French song from 1955.
Bécaud recorded his own composition as “Je t’appartiens.” It was issued in December 1955 in France on the EP “5 – Je t’appartiens,” La Voix de son Maître 7 EGF 171.

items.who: Gilbert Bécaud, Pierre Delanoë and Manny Curtis
items.why: Bécaud wrote the music and Delanoë the French lyric. Manny Curtis wrote the English lyric titled “Let It Be Me” — a separate piece of writing from the French words.

Corey sang Curtis’s English lyric on the television series Climax! in 1957; Columbia released it as a single and it reached number 57 on the Billboard Hot 100 — before the Everly Brothers recorded theirs.

misattribution.truthLine: Written and first recorded by Gilbert Bécaud as “Je t’appartiens,” issued December 1955 on La Voix de son Maître. The Everly Brothers’ famous version came in 1960.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: A French chanson does not usually cross the Atlantic intact. What crossed was the tune. Manny Curtis wrote an English lyric that kept Bécaud’s long, climbing melodic line but dropped the specificity of Delanoë’s French, and once a song is in English it stops sounding imported. By the time Cadence pressed the Everly Brothers’ single in 1960, the record most American listeners heard had no visible French ancestry at all — just two brothers from Kentucky and a title that sounds like it was always in English.

There is also an English-language recording that history skipped past entirely. Jill Corey sang the Curtis lyric on the CBS series Climax! in 1957 and Columbia released it as a single; it reached number 57 on the Billboard Hot 100. That is a real chart entry, three years of American exposure before the Everlys walked into a New York studio — and almost nobody remembers it.
detailsBody: 1955 — Gilbert Bécaud writes the music, Pierre Delanoë the French words, and Bécaud records “Je t’appartiens.”
December 1955 — the recording is issued in France on the 7-inch EP “5 – Je t’appartiens,” La Voix de son Maître 7 EGF 171, with orchestra directed by Wal-Berg.
1957 — Manny Curtis writes an English lyric, “Let It Be Me.” Jill Corey performs it on the television series Climax!; Columbia issues it as a single and it reaches number 57 on the Billboard Hot 100.
December 1959 — The Everly Brothers record the song in New York, with Archie Bleyer producing after recommending it to them.
1960 — Cadence Records releases the Everly Brothers single, backed with “Since You Broke My Heart.” It reaches number 7 on the Billboard Hot 100, number 8 in Canada and number 13 in the UK.
1964 — Betty Everett and Jerry Butler take it to number 5 on the Hot 100 and number 1 on the R&B chart; Glen Campbell and Bobbie Gentry chart it in 1969, Willie Nelson in 1982.
context.pull: The melody is French. The lyric everyone sings is not the lyric that was written first.
